# Amid Influx of 'Decompiled' Games, New Xbox Lab to Explore AI-Created Ports

PCMag · Michael Kan · 2026-10-13

A surge in people harnessing artificial intelligence to reverse-engineer classic video games—including running Halo in a web browser—has prompted Microsoft's Xbox to form a new lab to explore AI-created game ports, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced Tuesday.
Some enthusiasts and software developers have been using AI models to efficiently “decompile” classic games, a process that reverse-engineers the game’s computer code into a human-readable format. Doing so manually usually takes years.
This has enabled people to port video games to other platforms, including PC, macOS, and web browsers, and even modify the code, raising tantalizing possibilities and questions about retro titles and game development. Although publishers have already issued cease-and-desist letters demanding the content be pulled, it’s not hard to see a future in which gamers privately create and run AI-generated games at home. The same trend is emerging with AI-vibed coded software apps intended to take on legacy products.
“In recent weeks, we've seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support," Sharma tweeted today. "Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support.
“Perhaps more surprisingly, we've seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another,” she added, possibly alluding to a project combining Elden Ring with Super Mario 64. "These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry,” including how games are often exclusive or confined to certain platforms.
“While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life, and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models,” she wrote.
In response, Sharma is forming a small division called Xbox Labs that’s focused on the vague goal of taking “emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience.” She didn’t offer any concrete examples, but said, “We'll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating. I think Xbox has an important role to play here.”
Sharma added, “I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible,” suggesting she wants Xbox to at least explore the AI-enabled games, rather than merely try to block them. “Labs gives us a way to explore new technology that is game design-led without abandoning the work already underway."
For now, the new Xbox Labs site lets visitors enter their email address to receive- future updates. If you sign up, the site will send an email that says, “More experiments coming soon," and "We're building the first Xbox Labs experiments right now, and we'll email you as soon as there's something to play."
